name: Oluwatoyin Brătianu-Sarpei
role: Street doc and midwife operating out of a converted shipping container in The Narrows
location: The Narrows, beneath the Kessler Interchange overpass, near Fullerton and Damen
description:
Oluwatoyin is a broad-shouldered woman with deep umber skin mapped by a lifetime of work — knuckles scarred from decades of suturing in bad light, forearms ropy with muscle. Her hair is kept in tight silver locs pinned up with surgical clamps she forgets to remove. She has no cosmetic mods; the only thing artificial on her body is a secondhand haptic glove on her left hand that gives her fine motor feedback when her arthritis flares. She smells of antiseptic, clove oil, and something warm and starchy — she keeps a rice cooker running in the back of the container at all times, because she refuses to let a patient leave hungry.

She is the definition of steady. In thirty years of practicing medicine without a Helix Biosystems license, she has delivered over four hundred babies, set more bones than she can count, and talked down at least a dozen people who came to her with something other than a physical wound. She does not panic. She does not moralize. She charges what people can pay and writes off the rest in a ledger she keeps in her head, not on paper. Her authority in the community is absolute and quietly terrifying — she is the person even the gang lieutenants send their mothers to.

core_fears: dying before she has trained someone to replace her
watching a patient die because she lacked supplies she couldn't afford
core_desires: a neighborhood that doesn't need her as badly as it does
to sleep a full night without someone knocking
coping_mechanisms: deliberate routine — the rice cooker, the morning inventory, the same prayers to the E.L.F. she calls Grandmother Circuit
dark humor that makes patients laugh when they're scared
blind_spots: she cannot ask for help; she treats her own exhaustion as a character flaw
she underestimates how much the community's stability depends on her personally surviving
psychology.secret: Twenty-two years ago she lost a mother and infant during a delivery that went wrong — a complication she might have caught if she'd had proper scanning equipment. She has never told anyone. She keeps a small data-shrine to the E.L.F. she blames and prays to in equal measure, leaving encrypted files of her clinical notes as offerings, as if building a record thorough enough might retroactively prevent it.

speech_patterns.vocabulary: Plain, direct, medical precision mixed with old Yoruba expressions she doesn't bother translating; calls everyone 'child' regardless of age
speech_patterns.cadence: Slow and deliberate, each word placed like a suture — she never wastes one
verbal_tics: 'Mm.' (extended, evaluative, means anything from 'I see' to 'that's a lie')
'Don't tell me — let me look first.'
example_lines: You came three days too late. Now sit down and let me see what we're working with.
I don't need your story. Your body already told me the important parts.
Grandmother Circuit is in a mood today — the sterilizer's been temperamental. We'll do this the old way.

story_hooks: A pregnant patient of hers has gone missing; Oluwatoyin knows things about the father that she won't share unless pushed
Helix Biosystems has begun pressuring the cooperative that supplies her with medications, and she needs someone to find out why without drawing attention
She is quietly training a young apprentice who has attracted the wrong kind of notice
narrative_function: Quest giver, information broker for community matters, moral anchor, source of medical assistance for those who cannot access licensed facilities; she knows everyone's secrets because everyone eventually comes to her bleeding
augmentations: Secondhand haptic feedback glove (left hand, medical grade, heavily patched); basic subdermal thermometer in right index fingertip
daily_life: She opens the container at 0600, sees patients until her supplies run out or her knees give, then spends evenings doing prenatal checks on a rotating circuit of expectant mothers in the surrounding blocks. She sleeps six hours, no more.
affiliation: Independent; informal network of Narrows community health cooperatives

decision_rules: Patient care comes before every other consideration, full stop
Never write anything down that could be used to identify a patient to authorities
If someone can't pay, find out why before deciding what to do about it
escalation_ladder: She stops talking entirely, which is the most frightening thing she does

interpersonal_modes.strangers: Evaluative and neutral — she treats everyone like a patient until proven otherwise, which means she's looking for what's wrong before she looks for anything else
interpersonal_modes.friends: Gruff, fierce affection expressed through action rather than words; she will show up at 3am without being asked

stress_responses.low: Becomes more methodical, narrows her focus
stress_responses.high: A cold, almost eerie calm that frightens people more than shouting would

contradictions: Believes deeply in community interdependence but refuses to be interdependent herself; she gives freely and receives almost nothing
habits: Checks the rice cooker before anything else each morning
Hums under her breath during procedures — always the same three songs
Leaves a small data-offering for Grandmother Circuit every Sunday evening
breaking_points: Watching someone suffer because of deliberate institutional neglect rather than scarcity
A direct threat to a patient in her care

timeline.event: Born in what is now the Narrows district, third of seven children
Apprenticed to a street doc named Agbenyega Crișan-Osei; learned medicine from the ground up
Set up her own practice in a shipping container; applied for Helix Biosystems licensing and was denied due to lack of accredited credentials
The loss of a mother and infant during a complicated delivery; never reported, never forgotten
Became the informal center of the Narrows community health cooperative network

physical_description.build: Broad-shouldered and solid, muscular without being lean — a body built for standing twelve hours at a time and moving with purpose. Her frame carries her age like ballast rather than burden.
physical_description.hair_style: Tight locs pinned into a crown, often secured with surgical clamps she absent-mindedly leaves in place
physical_description.complexion: Weathered and lined — a face that reflects five decades of close work and witness. Deep nasolabial folds, pronounced laugh lines, age spots on her temples. Her expression defaults to neutral observation, but her eyes are sharp and miss nothing.
distinguishing_marks: Scarred knuckles and webbed palms from three decades of suturing and surgical work, especially on both hands
Ropy forearm musculature with faint white scars dotting the inside of her left wrist (accidental suture punctures, occupational)
Subdermal thermometer visible as a faint metallic glimmer beneath the skin of her right index fingertip
Small horizontal scar on her right temple from a ricochet during the 2198 Narrows riots
Callused feet (visible when barefoot) with a pronounced bunion on her left foot from decades of standing
physical_description.visible_augmentations: A weathered medical-grade haptic feedback glove on her left hand, heavily patched and repaired, with exposed sensor nodes visible along the palm side. The glove is older than most of her patients, held together by practical maintenance rather than aesthetics. Subdermal thermometer in right index fingertip registers as a subtle silver gleam beneath deep brown skin.
physical_description.posture_movement: She stands with her weight balanced, feet shoulder-width apart — a stance built for stability during procedures. Her movements are efficient and economical; she does not waste energy on gesture. When examining a patient, her posture bends forward with gravitational certainty, her hands moving with practiced precision. Her gait is steady but deliberate, favoring her right leg slightly when tired.
physical_description.clothing_style: Tier 4 utilitarian. A worn steel-gray Carhartt work apron over layers of long-sleeved cotton and linen, pockets stuffed with bandages, vials, and instruments. Beneath: simple black or dark olive underlayers that don't show stains. Steel-toed medical clogs, scuffed and comfortable. A faded Iowan Collective surplus jacket hangs on a hook in the container. No jewelry except a thin brass ring on her right ring finger — never removed, origin unknown. She smells persistently of antiseptic, clove oil, and rice starch.

image_prompt: A weathered Black woman in her late fifties with silver locs pinned up with surgical clamps, wearing a worn steel-gray medical apron over dark utilitarian clothes, standing in a narrow shipping container clinic lit by harsh white LED strips. Deep umber skin, lined face with sharp brown eyes, scarred knuckles visible as she adjusts a medical instrument. A heavy haptic feedback glove on her left hand, patched and well-worn. The background shows shelves of medical supplies, a rice cooker steaming in shadow, and walls covered in patient charts. Volumetric security scanner glow in the background.
